title: Knowledge exchanges: how to help prison officers learn from the best, and bring it back November 18, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: This Unlocked Graduates post argues that many prison officers have never worked outside their own establishment, and that visits, exchanges and conferences show them what is possible and give them the tools to change things back home. It recommends that every officer get the chance to learn beyond their own prison, that international exchanges be considered for fresh solutions to persistent problems, and that every visit be structured with preparation beforehand and a debrief afterwards. Evidence comes from the Unlocked Vanguard project, which took 25 officers to shadow colleagues in Swedish prisons, and from the 2024 graduate cohort, where over three-quarters strongly agreed that visits to high-performing establishments were a valuable chance to see good practice. A placement at a Big 4 consultancy is offered as an example of learning flowing both ways, as a participant helped the firm rethink how it supported staff with lived experience of prison. The post is practical coaching advice on turning an interesting trip into accountable change.
points: Seeing good practice in person is more powerful than reading about it, and it gives staff fresh eyes on their own establishment.
Exchanges work best when structured: each participant picks two challenges to look for before the visit and joins a debrief afterwards.
A structured debrief should end with specific changes to test and a plan for holding people accountable for trying them.
Exchanges can teach hosts as well as visitors: a participant's explanation led a consultancy to treat disclosure as the individual's choice and to recruit into ordinary teams.
quotes: Give every officer a chance to learn beyond their own prison. Offer visits to other prisons, prison exchanges and the chance to present at relevant conferences, to broaden experience and understanding.
Seeing what is possible in person is far more powerful than reading about it.

Unlocked has seen real value in hosting visits from prison staff working in other countries, and in taking frontline staff to see excellent practice in prisons abroad. As part of the Unlocked Vanguard project, testing our model in two London prisons, we took two groups of officers (25 in total) to Sweden to spend several days shadowing officers at Österåker and Täby prison.

As part of the 2024 Unlocked core graduate programme, in the cohort’s second year of training, all participants visited secure establishments identified by HM Inspectorate of Prisons as high performing. Over three-quarters strongly agreed that the visit gave them a valuable chance to learn different ways of working and see good practice.

During one placement at a Big 4 consultancy, a participant explained to their hosts what it means for someone with lived experience of prison to own that part of their identity. The firm had been hiring people with lived experience with good intentions, but had grouped them into a single cohort and made their extra support visible to colleagues.

This experience meant that I could return to my prison with 'fresh eyes' and a new sense of gratitude that we do have some scope for facilitating change. Participating in this exchange re-energized my motives for working on the frontline and helped me to continue building my confidence.
Preparation before a visit and structured reflection after it are what make it valuable.

Afterwards, a structured debrief helps turn an interesting visit into meaningful action. It lets participants consolidate learning, compare perspectives and work out what is genuinely transferable to their own prison.
